Q: Fitting an image inside CtkLabel A:

Something like:

The black bars are caused by CustomTkinter not handling RGBA transparency well, it renders the transparent pixels as black instead of showing nothing.

You don't need the rounded mask at all since your CTkLabel already has corner_radius=12 which handles the visual rounding for you. Just change your image to RGB and drop the mask entirely:

python

def _build_thumbnail_image(self, image_data):
    image = image_data.convert("RGB")
    image = ImageOps.fit(
        image,
        (272, 153),
        method=Image.Resampling.LANCZOS,
        centering=(0.5, 0.5)
    )
    return ctk.CTkImage(
        light_image=image,
        dark_image=image,
        size=(272, 153)
    )

Q: boost asio concurrent async_read and async_write A:

I think you are correct w.r.t. the documentation. I always use a single strand with sockets to make this threadsafe.

But this is not about async_read and async_write. Those a composed operations that call async_{read,write}_some member functions one or more times. Only those member function calls, of course, must be serialized. The operations themself may overlap. They do not happen "on the object" but in the system in the background.

So you can asynchronously read and write in parallel. Just not initiate those in parallel. The way to do that is use a single strand. Asio guarantees it will execute the intermediary _some calls in the same strand/executor that the final handler is executed in (the tokens bound/associated executor). That is the crucial part.

Q: Making the prefix 0o for octal numbers mandatory? A:

Tongue-in-cheek: Why not 0n for binary and 0t for octal (and 0c for decimal) so that the prefix always uses the third letter of the name of the base?

I agree that the historic case-insensitivity of the hex prefix (0x and 0X both being permitted) requires 0o and 0O to be treated the same (and also 0b and 0B). And the potential for mistakes with with 0O being overlooked are quite high. Personally, I use a 0x prefix and upper-case letters for hex output. The dip at the front of the number signals the prefix; the lower-case a, c, e add dips in the main number which A, C, and E do not. And 0b spoils that a bit (no pun intended), but I don't often write binary numbers.

Q: How can I specify environment variables for the VS Code process in my VS Code settings? A:

I'm not aware of existing VS Code settings that allow you to do this. I'm not surprised, since in general, you can't change the environment of a process that has already been started. See the following on unix.stackexchange.com for more info: change environment of a running process.

I suppose this could technically be implemented: VS Code could change its executable into a wrapper program which reads the VS Code settings file(s), then execs (without forking) the actual VS Code executable with modified environment variables from the settings. Feel free to raise a feature request and see if this is actually a legitimate idea (I'm not sure).

You can specify environment variables to add to the environment of a process when you start that process. See the env command.

Also related if you're using a shell like Bash:

  • Setting an environment variable before a command in Bash is not working for the second command in a pipe
  • How can I set an environment variable only for the duration of the script?
  • How set multiple env variables for a bash command
  • Setting environment variable for one program call in bash using env

Or, it may be acceptable to you to just modify your system environment, which applies to all processes started in the system by default. Related:

  • Setting environment variables on OS X
  • (askubuntu.com) How do I add environment variables?
  • for windows: (superuser.com) What are PATH and other environment variables, and how can I set or use them?

There's a slightly related feature-request about this here for the extension host process: API: allow an extension to change the environment variables #152806. See also this comment there about more broadly applying it to the "root" VS Code process, this update/summary, and this note about using process.env for the extension host.
